abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: DNA is a versatile abiomaterial for constructing nanostructures with biomedical and biotechnological applications. Among the methods available, DNA origami is a robust and widely recognized technique. Traditionally, most origami designs adopt antiparallel crossovers in both scaffold and staple strands, with less emphasis on parallel crossovers, which offer advantages like enhanced nuclease resistance and single‐strand routing potential. Here, a DNA origami nanostructure is designed, featuring two rotational panels that can be locked into configurations based on either antiparallel or parallel crossovers. By systematically varying the length and arrangement of these key staples, 36 pairs of antiparallel and parallel designs are studied in competitive folding tests, providing insights into the relative preference for each design. The 12 antiparallel and parallel designs are ranked, their folding pathways are examined, and nuclease resistance is assessed. The results reveal that the arrangement of staples near the central scaffold crossover is crucial for shifting between parallel and antiparallel conformations. Additionally, a two‐way isothermal transformation between antiparallel and parallel origami driven by toehold‐mediated displacement reactions is demonstrated, highlighting the potential of parallel designs as dynamic nanodevices for temperature‐sensitive environments. This study offers valuable insights into ‐ dynamics in antiparallel and parallel DNA origami, opening opportunities for designing nanodevices based on parallel crossovers.

This dynamic DNA origami features two rotational panels that can be designed into two major configurations using either antiparallel crossovers (AX) or parallel crossovers (PX). Through competitive folding processes, 36 pairs of designs with different key staples are studied, and a bidirectional isothermal transformation is demonstrated, providing insights for designing temperature‐sensitive dynamic DNA nanodevices leveraging PX configurations.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In this study, we developed a DNA origami design capable of adopting both AX and PX topologies by incorporating two rotational panels that can be configured in either a PX or AX arrangement through a 180‐degree rotation. We created a total of 12 origami designs, including six variations of PX‐based origami and six of their AX counterparts, by modifying the number and arrangement of central staples with different hybridization lengths. We systematically conducted 36 (6 × 6) competitive studies to compare the relative yields of PX and AX origami, allowing us to rank the 12 designs. Following this, we analyzed the folding pathway and nuclease resistance of the highest and lowest‐ranked PX and AX origami, as well as conducted a toehold‐mediated, isothermal transformation study between AX and PX designs. Our study expands the usage of PX topologies in origami systems and offers new opportunities for creating innovative origami nanostructures. Additionally, the reconfiguration study demonstrated useful applications for a dynamic nanodevice based on the isothermal transformation between AX and PX configurations.

sec.title: Competitive Folding of 36 Pairs of PX and AX Origami
sec.p:
By rotating the top and bottom panels of the assembled origami (Figure
1a), we created two distinct conformations of AX and PX nanostructures (Figure 1b,c), with their arms oriented in either the same or opposite directions. This was achieved by incorporating different sets of central staple strands. These central staples, highlighted in black (AX) and red (PX), were further categorized into two types within each color: 1) strands with a long hybridization length, or binding domain, of 1.5 turns (15 or 16 base pairs, bp) for joining the two panels through crossover formation, and 2) strands with a short hybridization length of 8 bp. Depending on how these central staple strands are arranged, the AX conformation can be shifted to the PX conformation, or vice versa, by rotating the top and bottom panels. The AX conformation is adopted when the central staple strands are oriented antiparallel, while the PX topology is formed with parallelly oriented central staple strands. Both the PX and AX origami designs include scaffold loops at the ends of DNA helixes to prevent potential base‐stacking interactions between origami structures, which could lead to unwanted aggregation (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information).

caption.p: Schematic representations, design details, and AFM images of AX and PX origami. a) Origami assembly scheme with a long, circular scaffold and numerous glue‐like small staples, colored in light gray that assemble the top and bottom body domains of the long scaffold, colored with orange and green tones, respectively. The zoom‐in box shows the central scaffold crossover in either AX or PX conformation. b) Two representative AX origami with long and short central AX staples and their corresponding zoom‐in details of the black highlighted central staples. c) Two representative PX origami with long and short central PX staples and their corresponding zoom‐in details of the red highlighted central staples. d) The AFM images of an AX origami design (e.g., A3) with zoom‐in images of the individual AX origami. e) The AFM images of a PX origami design (e.g., P3) with zoom‐in images of the individual PX origami. All scale bars are 600 nm. The zoom‐in images are 123 nm × 123 nm.

sec.p: These designed structures were assembled by mixing the long scaffold strand (M13mp18), the central staple strands, and the remaining body staples, followed by an annealing process using a short (≈1hr) temperature‐controlled program with a gradient in TAE buffer containing 12.5 mM Mg2+ (Section SI‐2, Supporting Information). The formed nanostructures were then confirmed using agarose gel electrophoresis to assess the size and compactness (or purity) of the target band, as well as atomic force microscopy (AFM) technique to visualize the origami structures with nanometer precision (AFM examples shown in Figure 1d,e).

To investigate the role of the central staples, we created 12 different designs (6 AX and 6 PX origami) by changing the number and the arrangement of central staples with different hybridization lengths (Figure
2a). These arrangements are properly designed to be comparable between corresponding AX and PX having the same hybridization lengths of the central staples across the same numbered designs (e.g., AX1, or A1, and PX1, or P1, as a pair), leading to a total of 6 AX/PX comparable pairs. First, we made sure that individual AX and PX origami can form the target structures without any formation issues based on AFM images (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information). We then tested the 36 combinations (6 × 6) of the AX and PX origami in the competing environment, in which a mixture of both AX and PX central staples was added to one assembly pot. The final assemblies were characterized by gel and AFM. AFM results of the tests were used for the yield counting in each combination (Figures S5–S16, Supporting Information). Using the counting dataset obtained from the AFM results, we summarized overall count ratios in percentages and placed them into a bar graph (Figure 2b; Table S2, Supporting Information).

caption.p: Competitive study of 12 AX and PX origami. a) Schematics showing 12 versions of AX (A1–6) and PX (P1–6) origami leading to 6 × 6 = 36 competitive combinations. b) A bar graph showing the % yield distribution of AX and PX origami in the 36 competitive combinations with the corresponding ranking of the 12 origami obtained from the statistics, from the highest (left) to the lowest (right) in terms of relative formation yields. The notations of AX and PX are simplified as A and P in the labeling of each origami design.

sec.p: Analyzing the yield statistics from the bar graph in Figure 2b, we ranked these 12 designs based on how preferable to be formed in a competitive assembly process. We first focused on comparing the 6 designs within each AX or PX pool. Our ranking is based on the average of all the relative formation yield (percentage number). For example, in the first group of Figure 2b, P1 formed against all 6 AX designs from A1‐6 at different PX%, as shown in Table S2 (Supporting Information). The average of the PX% is 35.5%. The average PX% of the other five remaining PX designs and the average AX% of all AX designs from A1 to A6 were calculated accordingly and were used to create individual ranking orders of PX and AX rankings: PX rankings based on the average PX% as P3 (38.5%) >P1 (35.5%)>P2 (25.1%)>P6 (20.0%)>P5 (14.5%)>P4 (3.5%) and AX rankings based on AX% as A3 (93.5%)>A2 (81.8%)>A1 (79.0%)>A5 (58.9%)>A6 (51.1%)>A4 (20.5%). After obtaining the individual ranking orders of PX and AX designs, we combined the two ranks together (Figure 2b). To merge the P and A rankings, we then compared each PX or AX design versus its 6 competing designs. The details of how to merge PX and AX ranking are included in Section SI‐6 (Supporting Information). The final merged ranking was found to be A3>A1≈A2>P3>P1≈P2>A5≈A6>P5≈P6>A4>P4.

As anticipated, the relative formation yields of origami designs, A3 and P3, were the highest within their respective AX and PX design pools. This success is attributed to their enhanced binding of the top and bottom body domains by 16 central staples with long hybridization lengths. When the number of central staples was reduced from 16 to 8, designs with long hybridization lengths, such as A1 and 2 and P1 and 2, outperformed their counterparts with shorter hybridization lengths, specifically A4,5,6 and P4,5,6. Among these, A4 and P4 ranked the lowest in their respective AX and PX pools due to the limited number of central staples with short hybridization lengths. A5 and 6 and P5 and 6 ranked as intermediates since they had a mixture of both long and short hybridization staples. In general, when combining the rankings of both AX and PX origami designs, the AX designs consistently ranked higher than their PX counterparts, suggesting a preferential formation of AX over PX conformation.

sec.title: The Effect of Central Staple Arrangement
sec.p:
To study the folding pathway of AX and PX configurations, we devised a new origami assembly scheme by arranging the long or short staples only near the central scaffold crossover or near the edge of the origami in both AX and PX configurations (Figure
3a). These staples were modified from the highest and lowest ranked designs (A3 and P3 and A4 and P4) and therefore we named the new origami according to the location of staples, including four with central staples (A3 in, A4 in, P3 in, and P4 in) and four with edge staples (A3 out, A4 out, and P3 out).

caption.p: Folding pathway study of two strongest and two weakest AX and PX origami (A3 and A4 and P3 and P4). a) Origami assembly scheme showing two possible pathways after mixing two competing sets of either outside or inside (middle) central staple strands of the A4 and P4 origami, respectively. b) AFM images showing the results of four different (2 × 2) competitive combinations with outside central staple strands of A3 and A4 versus inside central staple strands of P3 and P4. c) AFM images showing the results of four different (2 × 2) competitive combinations with inside central staple strands of A3 and A4 versus outside central staple strands of P3 and P4. d) AFM images of the competitive combination from the mixture of outside A4 versus inside P4 central strands and e) the labeling showing how the counting of the various conformations was done. The smaller scale bars in (b) and (c) are 100 nm, and the larger bars in (d) are 600 nm.

sec.title: Isothermal Assembly of AX and PX Designs Below Melting Temperatures

caption.p: Isothermal annealing and isothermal transformation study via competitive isothermal annealing with two strongest and two weakest AX and PX origami (A3 and A4 and P3 and P4) using TANa buffer containing NaCl. a) Origami isothermal annealing scheme of individual origami formation. b) An agarose gel result showing the assembled P3, A3, P4, A4 origami that were isothermally annealed with 2.5 nm scaffold and 25 nm staples (10x the scaffold) at 35 °C for 4 days in TANa buffer of 100 mM [NaCl] and c) their corresponding AFM images. All scale bars are 200 nm.

sec.title: Dynamic Transformation Between AX and PX Designs
sec.p:
To demonstrate the dynamic feature of our AX and PX designs, we implemented toehold‐mediated strand displacement reactions[
23
] to facilitate reconfigurations between the strongest and weakest AX and PX pairs, such as from P4 to A3 and A4 to P3. As shown in Figure
5a,b, the transformation into PX or AX conformations was achieved within 2 h, supported by 24 toehold regions in the central scaffold of the new origami designs. This was accomplished by modifying the original fully complementary central staples in A4 and P4, shortening them by 3 nucleotides at each end (design details in Figure S29, Supporting Information). The reactions were designed to convert these intermediate designs into fully complementary strongest designs, A3 or P3. The bar graphs in Figure 5a,b illustrate that increasing the number of toeholds from 0 to 24 significantly enhanced transformation efficiency, achieving ≈80–90% PX conformation and over 90% AX conformation within a few h (statistics in Table S6, Supporting Information). As expected, systems with 8 toeholds required 1 day to reach comparable transformations, with AX conformations more favored: transformation from P4 to AX reached ≈68% AX, while transformation from A4 to PX reached ≈50% PX. In contrast, non‐toehold systems showed no detectable transformation to the alternate conformation after 1 day. Extended experiments with non‐toehold systems spanning up to 7 days demonstrated a slow transformation process (Figure S26, Supporting Information), further highlighting the critical role of toeholds in accelerating dynamic transformations. All transformations were performed isothermally at 40 °C, underscoring the potential of these designs as dynamic nanodevices. These features highlight the applicability of our system for biological and biomedical applications, where rapid and efficient conformational changes are essential.

caption.p: Toehold‐mediated dynamic transformation from P4 to A3 and A4 to P3. a) Transformation from P4 to A3 conformation b) Transformation from A4 to P3 conformation. Each AFM image next to its corresponding group, including 24 toeholds, 8 toeholds, or no toehold (control), is from the 4‐h transformation, displayed as a representative image of each group. All scale bars are 200 nm.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In future studies, new PX design variations with increasing PX crossovers up to 100% and diverse topologies, including various 2D and 3D patterns with differing degrees of compactness, can be explored. These designs can be evaluated for their competition with AX counterparts and their nuclease resistance, aiming to expand the library of functional PX origami designs. Additionally, these studies will help investigate the factors influencing origami nuclease degradation, providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of nuclease digestion. As demonstrated by the toehold‐mediated, bidirectional transformation between AX and PX origami, our designs showcase their potential as a platform for creating dynamic nanodevices. These devices feature switchable on/off functionality achieved through shapeshifting between AX and PX topologies, making them ideal candidates for sensor‐like applications. The transformation process efficiently achieved dominant target conformations within a short timeframe, highlighting the versatility and effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, these designs can be combined with external molecules, such as fluorophores, to explore additional dynamic properties and expand the range of applications for AX/PX hybrid materials.
